<reflection>
After the second experiment with higher catalyst concentration (0.05 M), the cumulative negative log-likelihood (NLL) values show that mechanisms M9, M20, M3, M12, M14, M11, M17, and M16 now have the best fits (NLL around -42.74 to -42.71), while M7 has become relatively worse (NLL -41.66). The aim of the second turn was to spread out the NLL values by probing catalyst dependence, which was partially achieved as some mechanisms (e.g., M9, M20) now stand out, but many mechanisms still have similar NLLs, indicating that further discrimination is needed. The differences remain small, so no mechanism can be confidently ruled out yet.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To discriminate among the remaining plausible mechanisms, I propose an experiment with high substrate concentration (3.0 M), low catalyst concentration (0.005 M), and added initial product (0.2 M). This design targets multiple mechanistic features simultaneously:
- **Substrate inhibition**: High substrate will test for substrate inhibition as in M7 (S + catS <=> catS2), which should reduce the reaction rate relative to lower substrate conditions.
- **Product inhibition**: Added product will probe for product-dependent deactivation or inhibition (e.g., M12: P+cat=>inactive, M17: P+catS=>inactive), potentially slowing the initial rate.
- **Deactivation pathways**: Many deactivation steps (e.g., M11: S+cat=>inactive, M16: S+catS=>inactive) are substrate-dependent, so high substrate may accelerate deactivation, altering progress curve shapes.
- **Catalyst dependence**: Low catalyst concentration reduces dimerization effects (M2, M3) and makes deactivation less pronounced if it is second-order in catalyst, helping to isolate substrate and product effects.
This condition avoids extreme regimes (e.g., catalyst saturation or depletion) and introduces new variables (high substrate and initial product) that have not been tested in previous runs, maximizing information gain across the mechanism set.
</hypothesis>
